questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what makes an outcome an exercise of soft power
questions.stem: A city wins an international design prize for a public square built with local stone and craft. Which feature of this outcome is best described as soft power?

options.text: The city changed the law on building materials so that competing cities must follow the same rules.
options.misconception: describes legal harmonisation rather than attraction

options.text: The award makes the city's approach attractive to others, who may adopt it voluntarily.
The city used its procurement rules to make the winning design the only purchasable option.
options.misconception: confuses market exclusion with voluntary attraction

options.text: The city paid a fee to the awarding body, which then endorsed the design in its report.
options.misconception: mistakes a purchased endorsement for attraction

questions.explanation: Soft power works through attraction and voluntary adoption, not through compulsion. Harmonised law, procurement exclusion and purchased endorsement all involve pressure or payment rather than genuine persuasion.
questions.hint: Ask whether anyone was made to adopt the approach.

options.misconception: infers replacement from a change in membership size

options.text: The wider forum is failing, because it grew more slowly than the working group.
options.misconception: treats slow growth as proof of failure

options.misconception: denies that where decisions are taken matters

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a norm becomes an obligation for a specific owner
questions.stem: A ministry has adopted an international safety standard for bridges. Describe the steps that turn an international norm into an obligation for a specific bridge owner in a specific region.

answer.exemplar: The norm travels through several stages before it binds anyone at the drawing board. It is agreed internationally, received into domestic law or binding technical guidance by a ministry, and then applied through permits, inspection regimes, and codes that only a designated authority can issue. An owner becomes subject to the norm at the last of these stages, when an approved design or an operating permit is conditioned on meeting the standard, so that a design complying with an older rule becomes unusable. The interesting cases are the gaps: where domestic law adopts the norm only in part, or where a specific exemption or grandfathering clause is written in, the international agreement does not translate into an obligation on the ground.

questions.explanation: The path runs from international agreement, through domestic adoption, to a permit or approval that conditions a specific project. Obligations bite where enforcement acts on the owner, and exemptions or partial adoption break the chain.
questions.hint: Trace where the rule stops being text and starts being enforceable.

options.misconception: assumes reaching the threshold binds non-ratifying signatories

options.text: It is not bound by the convention's obligations, because it never deposited an instrument.
It is bound provisionally, because signing is treated as a form of provisional ratification.
options.misconception: treats signature as provisional ratification

options.text: It is bound unless it objects in writing, since silence is taken as acceptance.
options.misconception: invents a default of acceptance that the excerpt excludes

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that a signatory that does not ratify is not bound, so the entry-into-force threshold affects the ratifying parties rather than every signatory. Signature is not provisional ratification and there is no default of acceptance.
questions.hint: Find the clause that deals with signatories who do not ratify.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a norm cascade in a described sequence

stimulus.body: A national building code adopts a fire-safety clause that requires the same sprinkler detail used in three neighbouring jurisdictions. Two years later two more jurisdictions copy the clause, each citing the previous adoption rather than any new evidence, and a regional body then lists the clause as a recommended requirement for all members.

questions.stem: In the scenario above, what pattern is described?

options.text: A collective action problem, since each jurisdiction copied the others to avoid the cost of acting alone.
options.misconception: reads a sequence of adoptions as a cost-sharing problem

options.text: Hard-law coercion, since the regional body requires the clause of every member.
options.misconception: treats a recommendation as a compulsory requirement

options.text: Soft power, since the earliest adopter influenced its neighbours without any obligation.
options.misconception: labels an adoption sequence as an attraction-only mechanism

options.text: A norm cascade, where each new adopter follows the previous one and the sequence becomes self-sustaining.

questions.explanation: A cascade is a chain in which each adopter's decision is explained by the preceding adoption, and each new link makes the next more likely. The regional listing then consolidates the sequence; nothing here requires cost-sharing, compulsion or persuasion alone.
questions.hint: Ask what each adopter cited as its reason.

options.misconception: ignores that agenda design shapes the choices available in session

options.text: Its influence is decisive and legal, because it can alter the text of the standards being adopted.
options.misconception: invents a drafting power that agenda control does not include

options.text: Its influence is negligible, because members can submit additional items during the meeting.
options.misconception: assumes the ability to submit items neutralises the power to schedule them

questions.explanation: Agenda control works by determining which options are considered, in what order, and how much time each gets, which shapes outcomes without anyone voting to confer that power. Members' ability to submit items is an addition to a fixed schedule, not a substitute for control of it.

options.misconception: mistakes delegate numbers for influence in a technical negotiation

options.text: Wait for the presidency, hoping the city-state's turn will come with more authority.
options.misconception: assumes the rotating presidency confers lasting influence

options.text: Frame the approach as the shared interest of all members, so it survives even without a vote.
Offer funding for the secretariat, since financial support buys a place in the process.
options.misconception: assumes funding secures access to an agenda

questions.explanation: Small states typically gain influence by shaping the issue so that their interest is a general interest, because what everyone wants needs no special vote. Delegation size, the presidency rota and funding do not by themselves create standing on a technical question.
questions.hint: Ask how the proposal can be in everyone's interest.

options.misconception: treats the act of signing as evidence of verification

options.text: The rule is weak, because it depends on the honesty of those it constrains rather than on any check.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the gain a free rider obtains from a shared scheme
questions.stem: Ten practice studios share a cost of 200,000 for a shared materials library, and each studio saves 25,000 if all ten participate. What is the largest total saving a single studio could obtain by staying out while the other nine continue?

options.text: 10,000, because the free rider's share of the cost is divided among nine paying studios.
options.misconception: computes the shifted share rather than the free rider's gain

options.text: 200,000, because a studio that stays out keeps the entire cost for itself.
options.misconception: treats the shared cost as though the free rider received it

options.text: 225,000, because the free rider captures the whole budget plus its own share.
options.misconception: adds the budget to the free rider's saving without basis

options.text: 25,000, because the nine remaining studios still fund the library and the free rider keeps its own saving.

questions.explanation: A studio that stays out still enjoys the 25,000 saving that the shared library provides, because the other nine keep it running. The total cost does not transfer to the free rider, so the gain is the saving it would have paid for.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the mechanism and limits of soft power
questions.stem: A region's design approach is adopted by several other cities without any obligation or inducement. Explain what makes this an exercise of soft power, and what would weaken it.

answer.exemplar: Soft power rests on attraction rather than on payment, threat or legal compulsion: the approach is adopted because others find it admirable, useful or legitimate, and there is no instrument that could have compelled them. That makes the adoption itself evidence of the influence, since it is voluntary and unpriced. The mechanism is fragile in particular ways. It weakens if the approach is commercialised into a purchasable service, because payment substitutes for attraction; if it becomes associated with a distrusted government or sponsor, because credibility transfers; or if the practice is not actually open to others, because what cannot be copied cannot persuade. Soft power therefore depends on the availability of the idea and the credibility of its carrier.

questions.explanation: Voluntary, unpriced adoption by others is the signature of soft power, since no coercion or payment is involved. It weakens when the idea is sold rather than shared, when its sponsor's credibility falls, or when the practice cannot be copied.
questions.hint: Ask what the other cities would have done if they had refused.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which owners a domestic standard binds

stimulus.body: The ministry's guidance states that from the date of issue, structures covered by the standard must be designed and built in accordance with it, and that permits for those structures will not be issued until the design has been checked against the standard. questions.stem: Based on the guidance, which owner is bound by the standard and which is not?

options.text: All owners of structures, because the guidance applies to every structure in the country.
options.misconception: ignores the express exemption for existing structures

options.text: No owners are bound, because guidance is issued by a ministry rather than by parliament.
options.misconception: requires parliamentary enactment for administrative guidance to bind anyone

options.text: Owners of new structures are bound through the permit condition, but most existing owners are not.
Only owners who opt in are bound, because the standard is presented as voluntary guidance.
options.misconception: treats a permit condition as optional for the regulated owner

questions.explanation: The binding mechanism is the permit condition, which applies to new structures, so their owners are bound through it. Existing structures are exempt apart from defect cases, and the medium of the guidance does not decide whether it binds.
questions.hint: Ask through which mechanism a duty attaches to a particular owner.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the legal position of a signatory that applies a code

stimulus.body: An institute signs a code of practice on 10 April. The code requires each signatory to deposit an instrument of ratification, and provides that signatories which have not deposited by the closing date are treated as having signed only, without any obligation. A third body, a national regulator, signs the same code and states publicly that it will apply the code in its approvals, but also declines to deposit an instrument.

questions.stem: In the scenario above, what is the legal position of the national regulator?

options.text: It is not bound by the code, though its public commitment may make its approvals consistent with it.
It is bound, because a regulator that applies the code in practice has ratified it by conduct.
options.misconception: treats practical application as equivalent to depositing an instrument

options.text: It is bound, because the code has already entered into force for the other signatories.
options.misconception: assumes the threshold for others binds a non-depositor

options.text: It is not bound and must withdraw its public statement, since inconsistent practice breaches the code.
options.misconception: invents a duty to retract for a state that is not bound

questions.explanation: The code binds only those that deposit, so the regulator remains outside its obligations while signing and applying it. Applying a code in approvals is a matter of the regulator's own practice; it does not deposit an instrument or bind it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the regulator did the act the code requires.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a claim about the reach of a widely ratified convention
questions.stem: A reviewer claims that because 40 states ratified a convention, the convention now constrains the 15 states that signed but never ratified. Which evaluation is sound?

options.text: The claim is correct, because a widely ratified convention reflects a general rule of international law.
options.misconception: infers general customary law from the ratification count alone

options.text: The claim is correct, because the number of ratifiers makes the convention practically unavoidable.
options.misconception: treats practical pressure as legal obligation

options.text: The claim is partly right, because non-ratifying states must still respect the convention's principles.
options.misconception: invents an obligation to respect principles for non-ratifying states

options.text: The claim is wrong, because the convention binds those that ratified it, subject to any reservations they made.

questions.explanation: A convention binds the parties that ratify it, and the strength of the ratification count speaks to its authority rather than to its reach over non-parties. Whether a provision reflects general law is a separate argument that the count alone does not establish.

options.misconception: mistakes the final adopter for the source of the cascade

options.text: Jurisdiction A, because each link takes the previous decision as its stated reason.

options.misconception: treats a tight time slot as coercion

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the practical effect of an unread declaration requirement
questions.stem: A professional body's code says members must declare any project that could affect their own commercial interests. Declarations are filed and never read again. Explain the practical effect of this arrangement on the rule's value.

answer.exemplar: A rule that is filed and never examined asks the members it binds to police themselves, so its real force depends on the willingness of those same people to comply, and on nothing else. The arrangement therefore produces two false signals at once. Members may believe the rule is monitored and adjust their behaviour accordingly, while the body believes it has a safeguard in place and relaxes its own oversight elsewhere. Where a declaration is not read, a known conflict is as likely to pass unnoticed as a genuine one, so the file records the existence of a rule rather than any evidence about practice. The cheapest repair is not a bigger file but a routine step: a named officer who reads declarations, a published summary, and a defined response when a declaration indicates a conflict of interest.

questions.explanation: A declaration nobody reads creates the appearance of a safeguard without any of its substance, so the file tells you nothing about conflicts and the rule depends on self-policing. A named reviewer and a published summary would make it real.
questions.hint: Ask who reads what the members file.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how unaccountable agenda control shapes outcomes
questions.stem: A secretariat can set the agenda of a technical conference and is not answerable to any member for doing so. Explain how this position produces influence over the standards that emerge.

answer.exemplar: Agenda control operates well before any standard is drafted. The secretariat decides which submissions are scheduled, how long each is given, the order of the items, and which working groups are convened, and those choices determine which problems are treated as solvable within the mandate and which are quietly left aside. Because the secretariat is not answerable for these choices, the control is not corrected by members who might have preferred a different programme, and it persists even when the eventual text is adopted by consensus. The result is that influence is exercised without anyone appearing to exercise it: the standard reflects what was scheduled, timed and staffed, and the absence of any item on the agenda leaves no vote to contest and no decision to appeal.

questions.explanation: Scheduling, timing and staffing decide which problems enter the standards, and unaccountability means members cannot correct those choices. The influence shows up in the content of what is adopted, not in any vote about the agenda.
questions.hint: Ask what never gets discussed, and who decides that.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what distinguishes a cascade from independent adoption
questions.stem: A sustainability requirement spreads from a few early adopters to most national codes within a decade. Explain what makes such a spread a cascade rather than a sequence of independent decisions, and what makes it stop.

answer.exemplar: A cascade is identified by a link between the decisions: each adopter's choice is explained by the fact that others have already adopted, and the visible evidence of adoption lowers the cost of following. That is different from independent adoption, where each jurisdiction acts on its own evidence and the resulting convergence would be coincidental rather than causal, and it is different again from compulsion, where an obligation rather than an example produces the change. Cascades stop for reasons that mirror the mechanism. If a leading adopter reverses course and the reputational value of the norm collapses, followers have less reason to continue. If an adopter is compelled to comply, the norm stops spreading by imitation and starts spreading by enforcement, which changes its character even though the text does not.

questions.explanation: The mark of a cascade is that each adopter cites the preceding one, so adoption is sequential and self-reinforcing rather than independent. It slows when the example loses its value, when a leading adopter reverses, or when imitation is replaced by compulsion.
questions.hint: Ask whether each adopter acted on evidence or on the example of others.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the reach of a norm from its enforceability
questions.stem: An international standard on structural loading is used by 30 countries, but in only 4 of them does a breach of it lead to a penalty for the engineer who signed the design. Explain why the reach of a norm and its enforceability are different questions.

answer.exemplar: Reach and enforceability answer different questions: reach asks whether a rule is accepted and used as the reference point by the profession in a country, while enforceability asks whether a breach produces a consequence for a particular person. A standard can be universally cited, copied into national codes and taught in schools, and still leave the individual engineer exposed to no penalty, no professional sanction and no liability, because the state has decided to use it as guidance rather than as a rule of liability. The distinction matters because the apparent success of a norm, measured by how many countries cite it, tells you nothing about whether anyone is actually exposed for ignoring it, and policy that targets compliance has to work on the second question.

questions.explanation: Reach measures citation and adoption, enforceability measures whether breach has consequences for a specific person. A standard used in 30 countries can still expose no engineer, so counting users says nothing about compliance pressure.
questions.hint: Ask who pays when the rule is broken.

options.text: 120, because each certificate corresponds to one structure for the whole year.
options.misconception: counts annual certificates as if each covered one structure

options.text: 24, because 120 certificates at five checks each can cover at most 24 structures.

questions.explanation: Each structure needs five certificates, so 120 certificates can account for at most 24 structures, and the remaining 376 have no evidence of compliance at all. Presuming compliance, or counting annual certificates as full compliance, would hide the gap.
questions.hint: Divide the certificates by the checks each structure needs.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a drafting secretariat frames the standard
questions.stem: A standards body has a permanent secretariat that writes the annotated agenda, the background papers and the draft text for every working group. Explain how this arrangement shapes the standard that results.

answer.exemplar: Because the secretariat writes the background papers and the first draft of the text, members are responding to its framing rather than starting from their own. The questions it chooses to put in the papers determine which evidence is treated as relevant, and the structure of the first draft tends to survive, since amending a document already in circulation takes far more coordinated effort than accepting a set of propositions already written for you. Two further effects follow. Time allocated in the annotated agenda converts a priority into a fact, because an item given an afternoon and an item given a coffee break are not weighed equally. And the memory of the secretariat, which spans changes of membership and government, lets it keep the standard consistent across sessions in ways that members, negotiating on behalf of governments with short horizons, do not.

questions.explanation: Writing the papers and the first draft sets the frame members respond to, and the agenda turns stated priorities into allocated time. The secretariat's continuity also lets it hold a standard steady across changes of membership.
questions.hint: Ask what members are reacting to when they debate.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Sources of influence for a small state
questions.learningObjective: Compute a small state's share of drafted clauses
questions.stem: A small state contributes 3 of the 40 clauses in a standard negotiated by 60 states. What percentage of the clauses does it contribute?
questions.explanation: Three of forty clauses is 0.075, which is 7.5 percent of the total. Using 60 states as the denominator would ask a different question about how many states contributed, not how many clauses.
questions.hint: Divide the clauses contributed by the total number of clauses.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Draw a supported conclusion about voluntary uptake

stimulus.body: The assessment records that the university's open design course was taken up by practitioners in 14 countries, that no fees were charged, that the material was published under a licence permitting reuse and adaptation, and that several jurisdictions went on to make parts of the curriculum a requirement for public architects. The assessment notes that no formal request or sponsorship was made by any of the 14 countries.

questions.stem: Based on the assessment, which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The spread was driven by legal compulsion in the jurisdictions that made the curriculum mandatory.
options.misconception: treats later legal requirements as the cause of earlier uptake

options.text: The spread was voluntary and unpriced, with legal effect following later in some jurisdictions.
The spread was the result of an official request from the 14 countries, which the record notes.
options.misconception: contradicts the record, which states that no request was made

options.text: The spread was driven by the fee structure, because the free licence made the course attractive.
options.misconception: invents a fee influence where the course was free

questions.explanation: The uptake was free, unsolicited, and unlicensed as a condition, and only later did some jurisdictions give it legal force, so the causal order runs from voluntary attraction to legal adoption. A legal requirement cannot explain an earlier voluntary take-up.
questions.hint: Note the order of the uptake and the legal requirements.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a minilateral coordination pattern

stimulus.body: Three coastal cities sign a shared protocol on tidal flood defences and invite the 40 other municipalities in the region to use its design manual. Twelve municipalities adopt the manual, and the manual's drafting group keeps its membership to the three signatories while updating the manual annually. The manual is credited in national guidance as a useful reference, but no municipality is required to follow it.

questions.stem: In the scenario above, what pattern of coordination does this illustrate?

options.text: A universal rule, because national guidance refers to the manual for the whole region.
options.misconception: treats a reference in guidance as a binding requirement

options.text: A cascade, because each adopting municipality followed the previous adopter's example.
options.misconception: assumes an imitation sequence with no evidence of citations

options.text: Minilateralism, with a small drafting core and voluntary uptake by others.
A collective action arrangement, because twelve municipalities share the cost of updating the manual.
options.misconception: invents a shared cost that the scenario never mentions

questions.explanation: A small drafting core that keeps its own membership while others take up the result voluntarily is minilateralism, and the manual's status as guidance rather than requirement confirms that uptake is not compelled. Neither a cascade nor shared financing appears in the scenario.
questions.hint: Ask who writes the rules and who merely adopts them.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Select the rule that reduces the incentive to free-ride
questions.stem: A shared flood-warning system serves 20 authorities. Each gains 30,000 a year from it and would pay 18,000 if all contributed. Which change would most reduce the incentive to free-ride?

options.text: Tie access to the warning data to payment, so non-contributors lose the free benefit.
Ask each authority to pledge the same amount annually, since pledges make free-riding socially costly.
options.misconception: assumes pledges bind behaviour without any enforcement

options.text: Publish the list of non-contributors each year, since shame alone will change behaviour.
options.misconception: assumes reputational pressure alone reverses the incentive

options.text: Increase the system's overall budget, so that each authority's share is a smaller proportion of the benefit.
options.misconception: assumes a bigger budget reduces the relative value of free-riding

questions.explanation: Free-riding persists because the benefit is separated from payment, and the direct correction is to reconnect them so that non-payment costs something real. Pledges, publicity and a larger budget leave the incentive exactly where it was.
questions.hint: Ask what a non-contributor would lose.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of items that could be decided
questions.stem: A secretariat may put an item in a side room, which has no minutes and no decision, or in the plenary, which has a vote and a recorded outcome. If 6 of 8 items go to the side room, what percentage of the items that could be decided was decided in plenary?

options.text: 25, because 2 of the 8 items reached the plenary and 2 divided by 8 is a quarter.
75, because 6 of the 8 items went to the side room instead of the plenary.
options.misconception: measures against the items that never reached a decision

options.text: 50, because the secretariat split the items evenly between the two rooms.
options.misconception: invents an even split that the figures do not show

options.text: 12.5, because one item of the eight reached a recorded vote.
options.misconception: miscounts the plenary items in the numerator

questions.explanation: Two of the eight items reached the plenary, and 2 divided by 8 is 0.25, or 25 percent of the items that could have been decided. Measuring against the items placed in the side room would produce a different and wrong figure.
questions.hint: Divide the plenary items by the total number of items.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the mechanism that creates a duty for an owner
questions.stem: A national ministry adopts an international loading standard. Which step is most likely to convert the standard into a duty for a particular building owner?

options.text: Publication of the standard in the official gazette, which makes it part of national law.
options.misconception: treats publication as the source of the duty on any owner

options.text: A condition attached to the owner's building permit that requires compliance before approval.
The ministry's announcement that the standard will be enforced against non-compliant owners.
options.misconception: treats an announcement of enforcement as enforcement

options.text: Inclusion of the standard in the professional curriculum for newly qualified engineers.
options.misconception: confuses professional training with a duty on a given owner

questions.explanation: The duty attaches where enforcement acts on the owner, and a permit condition is the mechanism that does this. Publication, announcements of future enforcement and curriculum changes shape context but create no duty for a particular owner.
questions.hint: Ask what the owner must do to get permission.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of adopters that followed the pioneers
questions.stem: Three authorities adopt a shared public-procurement clause. A further five adopt it in the following year, and the remaining nine in the year after that. Of the 17 authorities that ultimately adopted it, what percentage came after the first three?

options.text: 17.6 percent, because 3 out of 17 is about 17.6 percent.
options.misconception: reports the pioneer share, which is the complement of what was asked

options.text: 52.9 percent, because 9 out of 17 is about 52.9 percent.
options.misconception: reports the final year's share instead of all later adopters

options.text: 82.4 percent, because 14 of the 17 adopters came after the first three.
100 percent, because all authorities eventually adopted the clause.
options.misconception: confuses eventual universality with the share asked about

questions.explanation: Fourteen of the seventeen adopters came after the first three, and 14 out of 17 is about 82.4 percent. Reporting the pioneers' share, the final year's share, or eventual universality answers a different question from the one asked.
questions.hint: Count everyone who adopted after the pioneers, then divide by 17.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Sources of influence for a small state
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a small state shapes text without votes
questions.stem: A small state has no vote in a standard-setting forum and no seat on its drafting committee. Explain the strategies through which it can still shape the text that emerges.

answer.exemplar: Influence without formal rights works through framing and relationships rather than through votes. The first move is to make an interest general: a proposal that answers a problem every delegation faces can be adopted by others who never mention the small state, which is the cheapest way to win a clause. The second is to work inside the drafting structure, supplying a technical annex that settles a question other delegates would otherwise leave open, because a text that already exists is far easier to adopt than one that must be argued from scratch. The third is to build a constituency in advance, so that when the clause is proposed there is already an interested group who wants it. The fourth is to exploit the venue, since agenda setters, secretariat staff and the chair control what gets discussed and how much time it receives.

questions.explanation: Small states win text by making their interest general, by supplying the technical drafting that settles a question, by building a constituency beforehand, and by using the secretariat and the chair. None of these depends on votes.
questions.hint: Think about how a clause travels without your name on it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute a net annual benefit after cost sharing
questions.stem: Six planning authorities share a coastal modelling service costing 360,000 a year, split equally among them. Each authority would save 75,000 a year in flood damage if the service existed. What is each authority's net annual benefit?
questions.explanation: The equal share is 360,000 divided by 6, which is 60,000 per authority, and 75,000 of avoided damage minus that share leaves a net benefit of 15,000. Reading the total cost as each authority's share, or the benefit as its share, produces a different and wrong figure.
questions.hint: Find each share, then subtract it from the damage it prevents.
